en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes, Section on the Ants.
8. The Question on the Limbs of a Cow “Venerable Nāgasena, as for what you said—that ‘four limbs of a cow should be adopted’—which are those four limbs that should be adopted?
“Just as, great king, a cow does not abandon its own home;”

In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga should not abandon his own body, [reflecting]: "This body is subject to impermanence, to being covered, to being rubbed, to breaking up, to being scattered, and to destruction.
This, Great King, is the first quality of the ox that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, when an ox has taken up the yoke, it bears the burden regardless of pleasure or pain.

In the same way, Great King, a practitioner, a follower of yoga who has undertaken the holy life, should practice the holy life until the end of his life, reaching even unto death, regardless of pleasure or pain.
This, Great King, is the second quality of the cow that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, when a cow drinks water, she does so with focused intent.
In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga, a yogāvacara, should accept the instructions of his teachers and preceptors, smelling them with zeal, affection, and confidence.
This, Great King, is the third quality of the cow that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, a cow carries whatever load is placed upon it.

In the same way, Great King, a practitioner of yoga, a yogāvacara, should receive with his head the exhortation and instruction of elder, junior, and middle-ranking bhikkhus, as well as that of lay followers (upāsakas).
This, Great King, is the fourth quality to be taken from the cow.
And this was said, Great King, by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:
‘Therefore, even one who has gone forth and is only seven years old from birth—
such a person too should instruct me.’
I accept it upon my head.
Having seen him, I shall establish in him intense desire and affection.
"One should place him in the position of a teacher, honoring him again and again.
Thus ends the eighth inquiry, the Question on the Limbs of the Cow.
